sections.heading: Coming to you because you have made yourself known
sections.text: God of love, I come to you with hope because of who you are. You have not left me to stumble around in the dark, guessing what you are like or trying to worship a God I cannot know. I cannot understand everything about you, but I do know this: you are good, ready to forgive, and rich in mercy.
theological_themes: God is not unknowable or hidden from those to whom he has revealed himself.
God's revealed character gives sinners real encouragement to come to him.
Human understanding is limited, but God's goodness and mercy are truly knowable.

scripture_references.connection: Paul contrasts worship of an unknown god with the true God who has made himself known and now calls people to repent. This supports the prayer’s confidence that God has not left humanity merely guessing about him.
This psalm grounds prayer in God's readiness to forgive and abundance of steadfast love. It fits the section’s movement from God’s character to the sinner’s encouragement to approach him.

sections.heading: Thanking you for creation and Scripture
sections.text: You have shown your wisdom, power, and goodness in everything you have made. And you have gone further: you have given your will in the Scriptures. You have preserved your Word, spread it, translated it, and made it available so that people like me can hear you, know you, and find the way back to you.
theological_themes: Creation displays God's power and divine nature.
Scripture is God's truthful revelation of his will.
The spread and preservation of Scripture are gifts of God's providence and mercy.

scripture_references.connection: Paul teaches that God's eternal power and divine nature are displayed in the created order. This supports the prayer’s gratitude for God’s wisdom, power, and goodness shown in his works.

Paul describes the sacred writings as God-breathed and able to make a person wise for salvation through faith in Christ. This directly grounds the prayer’s view of Scripture as God’s preserved and savingly useful revelation.

sections.heading: Seeing your glory and grace in your Word
sections.text: In your Word I see who you are: your greatness and your kindness, your compassion and your justice, your mercy and your truth. I also see what human hearts are really like, including my own. Through Scripture you have made your name known and have given the gospel to the world.
theological_themes: Scripture reveals both God's character and the truth about the human heart.
God's mercy and justice are not opposed in his revelation.
The gospel is a gracious gift to humanity through God's Word.

scripture_references.connection: Hebrews presents God's Word as living and discerning, exposing the thoughts and intentions of the heart before God. This supports the prayer’s claim that Scripture reveals not only God but also the reality of human hearts.
This passage shows God's righteousness, mercy, and truth coming together in the gospel through Christ. It illuminates the prayer’s emphasis on seeing both grace and rectitude in Scripture.

sections.heading: Confessing how poorly I have responded
sections.text: Have mercy on me. I have received your gifts with so little gratitude. I have wasted privileges others long for. I have treated spiritual things as if they were light and unimportant. I have ignored your messages, pushed back against godly examples, quieted the warnings of my conscience, brushed aside the concerns of faithful friends, and failed to pay attention when your providence was leading me. I have no claim on your kingdom as something I deserve.
theological_themes: Sin includes ingratitude, neglect of spiritual privilege, and resistance to God's gracious warnings.
God uses conscience, other believers, and providence to call people back to himself.
Kingdom privileges can be despised and therefore must not be presumed upon.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus warns religious leaders that the kingdom would be taken from those who rejected its fruit. The prayer echoes this sober sense that spiritual privilege brings responsibility and can be forfeited through unbelief and hardness.

Hebrews warns believers not to drift from what they have heard and not to neglect such a great salvation. This fits the confession of treating spiritual realities lightly despite receiving clear gospel privileges.
Paul describes conscience as bearing witness within people, sometimes accusing or excusing them. This supports the prayer’s confession of resisting the rebukes of conscience.

sections.heading: Turning to Jesus for mercy and change
sections.text: Lord, I confess my sin honestly and with grief. Give me a broken and humbled heart before you—not despair that runs away from you, but the kind of self-distrust that stops defending myself and comes to you for mercy. My hope is Jesus. Give me faith in him as Savior, forgiveness through his blood, strength from his nearness, and holiness by his Spirit. Teach me to love you with my whole heart.
theological_themes: True confession involves contrition, humility, and turning to God rather than self-justification.
Jesus is the sinner's hope for forgiveness, strength, and salvation.
Holiness comes through the work of the Holy Spirit, and the goal is wholehearted love for God.

scripture_references.connection: David teaches that God receives a broken and contrite heart rather than mere outward sacrifice. This grounds the prayer’s request for sorrow over sin that truly turns toward God.

John connects honest confession with God's faithfulness to forgive and cleanse, and he grounds cleansing in the blood of Jesus. This strongly supports the prayer’s appeal for forgiveness through Christ’s blood.
Paul prays that believers would be strengthened by the Spirit and know Christ's love deeply. This supports the request for strength by Christ’s presence and a heart enlarged in love for God.
Jesus names love for God with the whole heart, soul, and mind as the greatest commandment. This directly grounds the prayer’s final request to love God wholeheartedly.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The line 'I deserve that thy kingdom be taken away from me' draws on biblical warnings about despised spiritual privilege. In some theological traditions, language about the kingdom being taken away may raise questions about assurance or apostasy; the adaptation preserves the warning without implying that salvation is earned by performance.

The original assumes gratitude for the translation, publication, and multiplication of Scripture. This is historically shaped by post-Reformation Protestant concerns, but it is also a broadly Christian thanksgiving for access to God's Word.

The original’s language of 'self-abhorrence' and 'self-despair' is spiritually intense and can be pastorally sensitive. The adaptation keeps the force of rejecting self-justification and self-reliance while avoiding language that could be mistaken for hopeless self-hatred detached from Christ.
significant_interpretive_choices: I rendered 'not left to feel after thee in the darkness of my nature' as God not leaving me to stumble around guessing what he is like, because the original contrasts fallen human ignorance with God’s self-revelation rather than mere intellectual uncertainty.
I treated 'thy being and men’s hearts' as Scripture revealing both God’s nature and the true condition of humanity, including the praying person’s own heart.

I interpreted the list of resisted influences—godly examples, conscience, friends, and providence—as gracious means God uses to call a person back, not as separate sources of revelation equal to Scripture.
I rendered 'self-despair' as despair of self-defense and self-reliance, not despair of God's mercy, because the prayer immediately turns to Jesus as hope.
